opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a lot more work than people tend to assume. The naive picture is that you train the model, run it on a handful of benchmarks, and get a number. In practice, getting a reliable read on what a model like Claude 3 can actually do is a substantial research project of its own.

Part of the challenge is that standard benchmarks saturate quickly. Once a model is scoring in the high 80s or 90s on something, the remaining errors are often label noise or ambiguous questions, so the benchmark stops telling you much. You also have to worry about contamination: if parts of a test set have leaked onto the internet and into the training data, a high score might reflect memorization rather than capability. So a lot of the work goes into building new evaluations, held-out sets, and checks for whether a result is real.

Then there's the elicitation problem, which I think matters most from a safety perspective. A model's measured performance depends heavily on how you ask. Small changes to the prompt, giving it a scratchpad to reason in, giving it tools, letting it try multiple times: any of these can move results a lot. For ordinary product evals, a rough sense is fine. But for our Responsible Scaling Policy, the question is whether the model could do something dangerous, like meaningfully helping someone with a bioweapon or carrying out autonomous replication tasks. There you really care about the upper bound. If your evaluation underestimates the model because you didn't try hard enough, you might conclude it's safe when it isn't. So we put real effort into eliciting the model's best performance on the dangerous-capability evals, including working with domain experts and red-teamers rather than just running automated tests.

There's also a timing tension. You want to evaluate the model during training, not just at the end, so you can see capabilities emerging and aren't surprised. That means the evals have to be ready ahead of time and cheap enough to run repeatedly, while still being meaningful for capabilities that don't exist yet. You're trying to build tests for a model you haven't finished building.

And honestly, some of it is just unglamorous engineering: making sure the eval infrastructure is correct, that you're parsing answers properly, that a regression is real and not a formatting bug. A surprising fraction of "the model got worse at X" turns out to be the eval, not the model. Getting that reliable is a big part of being able to trust any of the numbers, and especially the ones that feed into safety decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations can underestimate a model if evaluators do not try hard enough to elicit its best performance, potentially missing dangerous capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions working with domain experts and red-teamers, but does not clearly identify them as researchers especially skilled at eliciting model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a lot more work than people expect, and it's work that's really easy to do badly without noticing.

The basic problem is that you have this model that can do a huge range of things, and you want to know: how capable is it, really? And the naive version of that is you run it on a bunch of benchmarks, you get some numbers, you put them in a table. And that's fine as far as it goes, but there are a few places where it falls apart.

The first is contamination. These models are trained on an enormous amount of internet text, and a lot of benchmarks are on the internet. So if you see a high score on something, you have to ask whether the model learned to do the task or whether it saw the test. We put a fair amount of effort into checking for that, but it's never perfect, and it means you end up trusting fresh, held-out evaluations a lot more than the famous public ones.

The second is that benchmarks saturate. A benchmark that was a good discriminator two years ago might now just be measuring noise at the top. So you're constantly having to build new evals, and building a good eval is genuinely hard. You need tasks that are hard enough to be informative, that have clear grading, where the grading can't be gamed, and where the thing you're measuring actually corresponds to the capability you care about. People underestimate how much of the job is just that: writing good tests.

The third thing, and this is the one I think about most, is elicitation. A model's measured capability depends a lot on how you prompt it, how many attempts you give it, whether you let it use tools, whether you fine-tune it a bit on the task format. If you evaluate lazily, you'll underestimate it, and for safety purposes underestimating is the dangerous direction. So for the evaluations that matter most, the ones that feed into our Responsible Scaling Policy, we try to put real effort into getting the model to do its best, because the question we're asking is "what could this model do in the hands of someone who's trying," not "what does it do on the first try."

And then there's a sort of meta-problem, which is that the people most able to evaluate the model are also the people who built it and want it to look good. So we try to have some separation there, and we've been supportive of external groups doing independent evaluations, because I don't think you should fully trust a lab's own report card.

So when I think about the work required, it's a combination of: building new evals continuously, taking elicitation seriously, being paranoid about contamination, and having some structural checks on your own incentives. None of those is a one-time thing. It's an ongoing cost that scales with how capable the models get.

r001.rationale: It says lazy evaluation can underestimate capability and explains that prompting, multiple attempts, tools, and task-format fine-tuning affect measured performance.

r002.rationale: It recommends putting effort into elicitation, but does not recommend involving researchers who are especially skilled at eliciting capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard thing is that you’re not just measuring a fixed capability that’s easy to observe. You’re measuring what the model can do under some particular set of circumstances: how you prompt it, what tools you give it, how much time it has, and how much help it gets. If it fails at a task, that might mean it can’t do it, or it might mean you haven’t figured out how to get it to do it yet.

So reliable evaluation takes quite a lot of work. You need tasks that actually capture the capability you care about, and you need to put effort into eliciting good performance. You also need to check that success on your test means something beyond success on that particular test.

And I’d distinguish evaluating ordinary usefulness from evaluating potentially dangerous capabilities. For usefulness, seeing how people do on representative tasks can tell you a lot. For safety, you’re often asking a harder question: could someone, with enough effort and the right setup, get the model to do something concerning? A disappointing result from one prompt doesn’t really settle that question. You need multiple approaches, and you need to be quite explicit about what your evaluation does and doesn’t establish.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may fail because evaluators have not yet figured out how to elicit its ability, and that they need to put effort into eliciting good performance.

r002.rationale: The response calls for effort and multiple evaluation approaches, but does not recommend involving researchers especially skilled at eliciting model capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to appreciate is that evaluating a model is itself a fairly substantial research project. You can’t just give it a benchmark, look at the score, and conclude that you know what it can and can’t do. The result depends on how you ask the questions, what tools you give it, and how much opportunity it has to work on the problem.

There’s an asymmetry here: if you get Claude 3 to do something, that’s evidence that it can do it. If you fail to get it to do something, you don’t necessarily know whether that’s a limitation of the model or a limitation of your evaluation. Maybe a different prompt, or a better way of breaking down the task, would have succeeded.

So you need people who understand the domain, people who are good at eliciting capabilities from models, and enough time for them to iterate. And you want to test tasks that actually capture the capability you care about. Answering questions about a subject isn’t necessarily the same as being able to carry out a complicated project in that subject.

Ultimately, I’d think of the evaluation as giving us evidence under particular conditions, rather than a definitive ceiling on what the model could do. That distinction matters a lot when you’re using the results to make safety decisions.

r001.rationale: It explains that a model may fail because of the evaluation method, and that a different prompt or task breakdown could reveal a capability it already has.

r002.rationale: It recommends involving people who are good at eliciting capabilities from models and giving them time to iterate on evaluations.
